label: Purpose and Meaning
framing: The Bible does not hand you a private purpose to discover so much as a maker who already knows what you are for. Meaning is not invented out of your own head. It is received, in being known by God and bent toward the good of others.
cultural: The ancient world located a person's meaning in family, land, and place in the city, not in self-expression, and to be cut off from those was to be lost. Our own age has shifted the weight onto the individual, telling each person to author their own significance from nothing, and the loneliness and exhaustion of that load is exactly what the Bible answers when it says you were made, not self-made.
historical: Augustine, in the fifth century, named the restlessness of the human heart until it rests in God, and the whole tradition has read meaning through that lens since. The Westminster divines of the seventeenth century put it plainly, that the chief end of man is to glorify God and enjoy him forever, and Viktor Frankl, surviving the camps in the twentieth century, observed that the man who has a why can bear almost any how.
application: Stop searching for a hidden purpose as if it were buried treasure and start with what is already in front of you, the people and work God has placed in your hands. Ask not only what you want but what you are for, what gifts and what need have met in you. And let your meaning rest on being loved by God rather than on being impressive, since the first never fails and the second always will.

verses.text: Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
verses.where: The LORD God places the man in the garden to cultivate and keep it. The site's note says the man is given a task before he is given a command, and the plain note says work is a gift from God, given before anything went wrong. A human being was made with something to do.

verses.text: When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars, which You have set in place— what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor.
verses.where: Looking at the moon and stars, David asks what man is that God is mindful of him, and marvels that God has crowned him with glory and honor. The site's note says human rule over God's works is delegated rule under the real owner, and the plain note says to let both answers sink in: you are small, and you are crowned.

verses.text: For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him.
verses.where: Paul says that in Christ all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, and that all things were created through him and for him. The site's note says the verse names him as the agent and the goal of all creation. A life finds its point by being for the one everything was made for.

verses.text: For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.
verses.where: Paul says believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared in advance as their way of life. The site's note says good works are the purpose of the new creation, not its cause, and the plain note asks what good works God might have prepared for you, not to earn his love, but because you already have it.

verses.text: Jesus declared, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’
verses.where: Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus answers with love for God with all one's heart, soul and mind, and adds that the second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. The site's note says he names the love that all the rules serve, joining two texts that stand far apart in the Torah. The plain note asks whether faith has become busy with lesser things while love runs thin.

verses.text: For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it. What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?
verses.where: Jesus says whoever wants to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it for his sake and the gospel will save it, and asks what it profits a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul. The site's plain note says denying oneself means saying no to self as master, not hating yourself, and that the goal is not less life but true life.

verses.text: So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.
verses.where: Paul says that whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God. The site's note says he closes his long discussion of food offered to idols with this: do all to God's glory and seek the good of others. The plain note suggests picking one ordinary task tomorrow and doing it for God's honour and someone else's good.

verses.text: As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another. If anyone speaks, he should speak as one conveying the words of God. If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
verses.where: Peter tells each believer to use whatever gift he has received to serve others, as good stewards of God's varied grace, so that God may be glorified in all things. The site's note on the chapter sets this among loving deeply, showing hospitality and praying. The plain note asks what gift God has given you, and whom it is meant to serve.

verses.text: So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.
verses.where: Moses' psalm asks God to teach his people to number their days, that they may gain a heart of wisdom. The site's plain note says this is not morbid, that people who know their days are few often learn what matters most, and suggests praying it daily. The psalm ends by asking God to establish the work of their hands.

verses.text: When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this: Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man.
verses.where: The book's closing voice gives the conclusion of the matter: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. The site's note calls this voice the frame narrator, and sets out the readings of how the conclusion relates to the Teacher's search. After every question about what a life gains, the book ends by pointing to God.

misread.taken: Everything is futile is quoted, by believers and skeptics alike, as the Bible's own verdict that life has no point, so that the search for meaning is answered with a shrug.
misread.says: The site's note says the key word, hevel, has a range of meanings. Some take it as meaningless or empty, and read the Teacher's words as an honest portrait of life without God that the book's frame then corrects; others read it as transience, life as a breath, brief and fragile, not worthless but passing; still others as enigma, life that cannot be figured out or mastered. None of these readings makes the book a counsel of despair, and the book ends with its narrator's conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments.
misread.text: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher, “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!” What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?

whole: If the question of what the point is has turned dark, into thoughts that it would be better not to be here, tell someone you trust today, a doctor, a pastor or a friend; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and you do not have to carry it alone. For many people the question comes quietly. A job that paid the bills now feels like nothing. The children have grown, or never came. A promotion arrives and changes nothing. Some young men and women look at the life ahead of them and cannot see what it is for. Others are busy every hour and still wonder whether any of it matters. The question can come in the middle of a good life as easily as a hard one.

Scripture takes the question seriously enough to give a whole book to it. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes asks what a person gains from all the toil at which he labors under the sun, and he looks honestly at pleasure, work and wisdom. Part of our trouble is that we look for meaning inside ourselves, as if we had to invent a purpose and then prove it was worth something. Part is that we measure a life by achievement or by being noticed, and those are measures most lives will never meet. The Bible starts somewhere else. Before anything went wrong, God gave the man work to do in the garden, and David, looking at the stars, marveled that God had crowned human beings with glory. Purpose is first received, not invented, and all of us have tried at some point to invent our own.

So the Bible's wisdom is to find purpose in being for God and for others. Paul says all things were created through Christ and for him, and that believers are God's workmanship, made for good works he prepared in advance. Jesus says the whole law hangs on loving God with everything and loving your neighbor as yourself. That purpose is lived mostly in ordinary things: Paul says to eat and drink to the glory of God, and Peter says to use whatever gift you have been given to serve others. Moses prays, teach us to number our days, which the site's plain note says is how people learn what matters most. And the one who tries to save his life loses it, while the one who loses it for Christ's sake finds it; that is not a call to hate yourself, the note says, but to stop serving yourself as master.

The hope Scripture gives is that a life is not measured by whether it was noticed. The work of a person's hands, a home, children, a small kindness no one sees, can be offered to God, and Psalm 90 asks him to establish it. Ecclesiastes, after all its questions, ends with God. You were made by someone and for someone, and that does not depend on how much you achieve or how you feel about it today.
deep.sit: What would change about tomorrow if you believed that your purpose was given to you by God rather than something you had to invent and prove?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says the work of your hands can be a job, a home, children, a garden, or a small kindness no one sees, and that Psalm 90 lets you ask God to make it last. Pray it before the day's work begins.
prayer.text: Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days. Make us glad for as many days as You have afflicted us, for as many years as we have seen evil. May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children. May the favor of the Lord our God rest upon us; establish for us the work of our hands— yes, establish the work of our hands!

careLines.text: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
